head_commit.message:
test(crypto): external conformance vectors for the crypto primitives

Adds crates/nightfall-crypto/tests/external_vectors.rs, which pins
each primitive nightfall-crypto depends on against vectors published
by that primitive's own specification.

CONTRIBUTING.md names "Independent review of the cryptography" as
the most valuable contribution anyone could make right now.
docs/AUDIT-READINESS.md section 6 item 4 names test vectors as one
of the three inputs an external auditor needs but which do not exist
today. This is that input.

Covered, with an explicit citation in each doc comment:

- BIP-39 — Trezor reference vectors.json (entropy to mnemonic).
  Three vectors plus a round-trip: same entropy yields same address.
- BLAKE3 — official BLAKE3-team test_vectors.json.
- Ed25519 — RFC 8032 section 7.1, TEST 1 (empty message).
- X25519 — RFC 7748 section 6.1 (Alice/Bob key exchange, shared secret).
- XChaCha20-Poly1305 — draft-irtf-cfrg-xchacha-03 section A.1: full
  AEAD vector (key, nonce, AAD, plaintext, ciphertext, Poly1305 tag).
- Nightfall's own hash_multi length-prefix property, the property
  CONTRIBUTING.md names explicitly.

Deliberately not covered, and why, in the file header:

- Nightfall's Schnorr-over-Ristretto has no external vector — the
  construction is generator-parameterised and H is domain-derived.
- Bulletproofs in Nightfall's parameter set is likewise
  Nightfall-specific.
- Argon2id at the RFC 9106 section 5.3 level uses Secret[8] and
  Associated data[12], which the stable argon2 0.5 API does not
  expose. Nightfall's nighthash wrapper keeps its own coverage in
  pow.rs; a follow-up can add the RFC vector once the crate exposes
  the low-level entry point.

The file header also states plainly what this is not: not an audit,
not a substitute for one, and not a claim that Nightfall's *use* of
the primitives is correct. Finding I-01 in docs/AUDIT-2026-08-16.md
is explicit that no internal document can take that role.

No new dependency, no new API, no consensus change. This commit
contains exactly one new file.

Tests: 11 passed in 0.02s. cargo fmt and cargo clippy --all-targets
clean.

head_commit.message:
docs: add audit readiness document

Adds docs/AUDIT-READINESS.md, the input document an external
security firm needs before it can quote a fixed-price
engagement: agreed scope, security invariants, attack surface
map, prior audit references.

Why: the repository has three internal review documents
(AUDIT-2026-08-12/-16, -09-08) and none of them is an outside
audit. The 2026-08-16 document says so explicitly, finding
I-01: "This document is not an outside audit." This document
does not perform an audit. It makes one possible.

Contents:

- Proposed scope in three phases: crypto core (~2,500 lines),
  ledger and consensus, node and P2P surface.
- Security invariants with file references: supply equation,
  range proofs, signature canonicality, stealth unlinkability,
  state transition atomicity, chain selection by work.
- Attack surface map (10 rows), each pointing at a specific
  file and threat.
- The 11 open items from the internal 2026-08-16 review, each
  marked as a candidate for external review.
- Known structural gaps: no formal verification, no
  third-party fuzzing, no cross-implementation differential
  testing.
- The six inputs an external auditor needs before bidding —
  three exist today, three do not.

Documentation only. No code, no dependency, no consensus
change. Orthogonal to all currently open PRs.

head_commit.message:
light-verify: independent header chain and PoW verifier

Adds crates/nightfall-light-verify, a standalone header-chain
verifier that walks headers and checks block linkage, height
continuity, proof of work against declared difficulty,
difficulty floor, and cumulative work — without importing
nightfall-consensus, nightfall-ledger, nightfall-node,
nightfall-storage, nightfall-wallet, or nightfall-p2p.

The cryptographic primitives (nighthash, meets_difficulty,
hash_multi, domain::BLOCK, Commitment) are shared with
nightfall-crypto. Re-implementing Argon2id would not add
security value — what matters is that the *rules* on top of
the primitive are derived twice. This is documented in the
crate-level doc comment.

Public API:

- HeaderView — wire-layout of a block header
- verify_chain(headers, config) -> Result<VerifiedChain, VerifyError>
- chain_is_heavier(a, b) -> bool
- VerifyError — one variant per rejection reason

Tests: 11 unit tests, all green in under one second. The
tests cover empty chain, single header, linkage, height
gaps, monotonic timestamps (and the option to disable that
check), difficulty floor, cross-difficulty work accumulation,
and heaviness comparison.

Motivation: RFC docs/RFC-LIGHT-VERIFY.md Phase 1. This PR
implements that phase. No consensus change, no new
dependency at the workspace level.

Out of scope for this PR: UTXO membership (depends on #20/#21),
scan completeness, Merkle-sum commitments. Those are later
phases of the same RFC.

head_commit.message:
docs: RFC for confidential supply certificate

Adds a design document for a verifiable supply certificate that
allows any light client, web wallet, or independent auditor to
prove Nightfall's global supply invariant holds, without
downloading the full chain and without trusting any node.

Documentation only. No code, no dependency, no consensus change.

Motivation: the official website documents that the web wallet
takes chain data from a configured node, and that a node can
therefore misrepresent the wallet's view. The supply invariant
is the only guarantee against inflation, and today only a full
node can verify it.

Defines a three-layer mechanism (Merkle-sum UTXO tree, UTXO
membership proofs, supply certificate) and a five-phase roadmap.
Phases 2 and 3 do not require consensus changes; Phase 4 requires
a hard fork and depends on PRs #20/#21.

This RFC expands Phase 4 of RFC #31 (proof-carrying light client)
into a standalone design with its own security analysis.

head_commit.message:
docs: RFC for long-term survival (quantum + regulatory)

Adds a design document covering two dated, external threats
that will affect Nightfall within 24 months and 10 years
respectively, and that have no documented response in the
repository today.

Threat 1: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 takes effect on 10 July
2027 and restricts regulated crypto-asset service providers
in the EU from holding anonymity-enhancing coins. Nightfall
already has the primitive the regulation asks for (view
keys, documented on the website), but it is not described
in a form a regulator can audit.

Threat 2: Zcash announced in May 2026 that it will be fully
post-quantum within 12 to 18 months. Monero is moving toward
Seraphis and Jamtis. Ethereum targets 2029. Nightfall's
cryptography is entirely ECDLP-based with no documented
migration path.

Documentation only. No code, no dependency, no consensus
change. Defines five phases: quantum-recoverable wallets
(no consensus change), selective-disclosure receipts (no
consensus change), hybrid transactions (soft fork),
post-quantum commitments and range proofs (hard fork),
and deprecation of the ECDLP path.

Phases 1 and 2 require no protocol change and could be
implemented independently of the later phases.

head_commit.message:
crypto: property tests for Schnorr sign/verify

Adds 9 property tests that exhaustively walk the malleability and
canonicality boundary of Schnorr signatures. No new dependency:
rand is already a direct dependency of nightfall-crypto.

Coverage:
- every single-bit flip in s (256 variations) must invalidate
- every single-bit flip in r (256 variations) must invalidate
- non-canonical s (>= group order l) must be rejected, not reduced
- s = 0 must be rejected
- r = identity must be rejected
- 128 random garbage (r, s) pairs must never panic
- empty message roundtrips
- 64 KiB message roundtrips
- 64 independent (secret, message) pairs roundtrip

The existing five unit tests remain untouched; total 14 tests green
in under one second.

On startup, roll back an uncommitted append only after authenticating the committed prefix against the previous local validation record. This avoids misclassifying a complete rewrite beside stale metadata as an append tail.

Full archive rewrites are also synced before publication. Pruned multi-file transactions remain a separate follow-up.

head_commit.message:
1.0.1: a wallet with no scan anchor must not stall forever

Every wallet written by 0.9.5 lacks the scan anchor 1.0 introduced, and
scan_blocks refuses an incremental page from such a wallet. That refusal
is correct; asking for the same refused page every thirty seconds while
reporting "Catching up" was not, and it left every upgraded wallet
frozen at the moment of the upgrade.

An anchorless wallet is now offered a single canonical pass from its
birth height — the repair the wallet already implements and the only one
it treats as sound — which writes the anchor and restores ordinary
paging. No coins were at risk: the refusal preceded any save.

workflow_runs.display_title: 1.0.0: atomic swap withdrawn, encrypted Vault, new wallet interface

head_commit.message:
1.0.0: atomic swap withdrawn, encrypted Vault, new wallet interface

Atomic swap is removed from the product. It was built and reviewed, and
withdrawn before release because the loss cases are properties of the
chain rather than defects: Nightfall has no script language, so a NIGHT
lock cannot refund itself on a timer the way a Bitcoin lock can. A
counterparty who cancels and stops acting leaves NIGHT locked with no
key and no timer; a redeem published too late discloses its secret while
the cancel confirms. docs/SWAP-WITHDRAWN.md is the full record.

Gone with it: the nightfall-swap crate, sixteen files across the core,
ledger and crypto crates, every call site, and 21 packages from the lock
file including all of secp256k1, the bitcoin family, and a second
implementation of the curve arithmetic the chain already uses. The
swap_journal field stays: the wallet database refuses unknown fields, so
removing it would make any file containing records unopenable.

No consensus rule, protocol version, genesis parameter or emission value
changed. There is no fork and no migration.

1.0.0 ships the encrypted Vault, Recovery Studio, encrypted backups,
invoices and receipts, Air offline signing and the rebuilt window.

head_commit.message:
A row that cannot fit widens its parent, and the next row takes the room

Measured on the Dashboard at 1400 points: the five activity rows in the
left-hand card came out 407, 432, 455, 475 and 495 points wide inside a
382-point card, fanning out to the right until the last one ran 72 points
under the card beside it. It read as two overlapping cards, which is what
it was.

The cause was fixed column widths. The amount column was 150 points
whatever the card was and the middle column had a floor of 90, so in a
narrow card the three parts added up to more than the row had. An
overflowing child widens its parent, so every row after the first saw
more room and used it. The columns are now shares of what there is, and
they add up to exactly the inner width — a narrow card gets a narrow
amount column instead of a broken layout.

Also:

- Notice fills were `gamma_multiply`, which lowers the alpha rather than
  mixing the colour, so they were see-through. The page banners are drawn
  above the scroll area, so the balance card slid underneath one and its
  buttons showed through the warning. `theme::tint` mixes an opaque tint
  instead, and every notice uses it.
- Card shadows had a 24-point blur while the column gap was 16, so each
  shadow crossed the gap and lay over its neighbour's border. Blur halved,
  gap widened past it.
- Outgoing payments are tinted red rather than neutral white. Sent looked
  like a note rather than a movement.

Three tests added, and the first version of one of them was wrong in a
way worth recording: it read `ui.min_rect()` after each row, which is the
running total of everything drawn so far, so it reported the same width
whatever the rows did — and passed while the screenshot plainly
disagreed. Each row is measured in its own scope now.

head_commit.message:
Air: paying from a wallet that is never on a network

The split is not the one a Bitcoin wallet has. A Mimblewimble transaction
cannot be built without the spender's outputs and their blinding factors,
and those come from the seed — so there is no useful "watch-only builds,
cold device signs" arrangement. The cold side holds the wallet; the
online side holds the node.

Two packages cross and nothing else does. An Intent goes out: what to
pay, to whom, at what fee, at what height, on which network. No secret in
it, so a photograph of one on a café table costs nothing. A Signed
package comes back: the finished transaction, opaque to this module,
which carries it and proves it arrived whole.

The signer checks for itself. It parses the intent into an address, a
whole number of darks and a fee, shows those, and builds the transaction
from the same parsed values. There is no path where the string displayed
and the values signed come from different places.

Replay goes wrong in three ways, so it is refused in three places: a
signed package quotes the nonce of the intent it answers; the online side
keeps a bounded log of nonces it has broadcast, so a QR left on a screen
and photographed twice is refused the second time; and the network is
checked on both sides, because a testnet intent signed by a mainnet
wallet spends real coins and nf1… is the same string on every network.

Every frame carries the digest of the whole payload, not of itself. A
per-frame checksum tells you a frame was read correctly; it does not tell
you the frames belong together, and splicing two transfers in front of
one camera is the failure worth preventing.

The size budget came from the end-to-end test rather than from taste: it
was 12 800 bytes and the first real transaction it was given was 15 908.

Not built: the camera. Core cannot see one, so the return journey is a
paste or a file. The frames are for a phone to read and the phone side
does not exist — which is written on the card rather than left for
someone to discover holding a transaction they cannot move.

Walk the remaining pages, and stop asking a settled invoice a question

Seen on a real till: an invoice marked Paid still carried "1 payment for
this amount arrived without quoting the reference". A candidate is the

  from its own label: "Send" at 75 points beside "Receive" at 92, which

  because four-across needed 880 points and a card has about 820 — a

head_commit.message:
The cards were darker than the page they sat on

BG was #423858 and SURFACE — the card fill — was #302747. A dark
interface reads a card that catches less light than its background as a
hole rather than an object, so every screen looked flat and unfinished
however its contents were arranged. It was one line, across eight pages.

The elevation ladder now runs one way: page, rail, card, control. Text
fields are the deliberate exception downwards, because a field is
something you put something into.

With it, the things that made the wallet read as a prototype:

- one control height instead of two, so a primary and a secondary button
  in one row stop sitting four points out of line, and buttons that are
  one decision share one width
- text fields with a radius of their own, sunk into the card rather than
  raised off it, and a label that stays — the label used to be the
  placeholder, so a half-filled form was a column of anonymous boxes and
  the only way to learn what one was for was to empty it
- a header bar on the full-window screens, which opened with a bare
  label in the corner and a card floating in a window more than half
  empty
- content columns that grow with the window instead of asking for 620
  points on any display
- the scan warning as one expandable line rather than three lines
  repeated on all eight pages
- the page description as a subtitle under the page title rather than a
  sentence floating between cards

Found by running it: a disabled primary button almost indistinguishable
from an enabled one, which answered a press with nothing at all and so
read as broken rather than incomplete — it stays live and names what is
missing; an onboarding screen taller than the window with no scroll
area, so "Cancel setup" sat below the bottom edge and a person part-way
through creating a wallet could not back out; the till's three fields on
three different baselines, because three fixed widths in a wrapping row
produce three different top edges.

The layout tests caught four real overflows during the rebuild, one of
them a row that added its own gaps on top of the ones egui inserts and
came out exactly two spacings too wide.

Also: a development build may now open mainnet, but only if it was
compiled to. The permission belongs to the artifact, not to a command
line, so a copy that escapes cannot be talked onto the real network by
an argument.

head_commit.message:
Counter: a till that does not guess

A merchant writes an invoice, hands out the request it produces, and the
till says where that one stands.

The rule the module exists to enforce: an invoice is never settled by an
amount. A payment settles an invoice only when its memo quotes that
invoice's reference, exactly.

Matching on amount would mean a till holding two invoices for the same
figure closes whichever it looks at first, and then asks the other
customer to pay again for money that has already arrived — silently, and
looking correct throughout. A payment for the right figure that quotes
nothing is shown as a candidate, counted, and applied to nothing.

A deadline is the merchant's policy, never a rule. A late payment
settles and is flagged as late: the coins really arrived, and a till that
said "expired" while holding the customer's money would be lying about
the only thing that matters. Closing by hand records a reason and does
not invent a payment, so the takings total only counts what really came
in and a day that does not reconcile is found at the end of the day.

Everything here is computed from what a view key can see. Nothing touches
a spend key: a till sits on a shop counter, which is the least defensible
computer a business owns. That is true of the code today, not yet of a
deployment — it is kept true from the start because it is hard to add
later.

Found by a test rather than by reading: the legacy-database reader
dropped the invoices, and its strict field list made migration fail
outright for any wallet that had used Counter. The mistaken assumption
was written down in a comment — that a legacy database predates the till
— and it is wrong, because the legacy backend is a current build writing
a plaintext file. A merchant would have lost their open invoices at the
moment they encrypted their wallet.

head_commit.message:
A receipt now reports what it proved, not just that it verified

verify_receipt returned (). Every screen then printed the receipt's own
fields, which is a different set from the fields that were checked.

Two consequences, both real:

A version 1 signature covers six of the ten fields. `kind` and
`timestamp` are not among them, so a valid receipt could have "sent"
rewritten to "received" — turning the signer's own word about an amount
into an apparent proof of one — and verification still returned success.
Version 2 signs every field the document displays, under its own domain
so a v1 signature cannot be replayed as a v2 one. Version 1 stays
verifiable: people may hold receipts for payments already made, and
breaking those would destroy the only evidence they have. The report
lists the fields the signature does not cover, and callers must show it.

A sent receipt carries no blinding factor and no commitment — its
`commit` field is a transaction id — so it proves nothing about an
amount beyond the signer's own word. That is far weaker than a received
receipt and nothing said so. `amount_proven` now carries the difference.

verify_receipt returns a ReceiptProof: what was checked, the one-sentence
summary, and what remains open. Chain inclusion is always in the second
list, because verification never contacts a node and a wallet that
blurred the two would present a signed sentence as a settled payment.

head_commit.message:
One amount, read the same way in every wallet

Core, the browser wallet and the mobile wallet each carried their own
decimal parser, and the copies had drifted:

    typed | Core    | browser   | mobile
    .5    | error   | 0.5 NIGHT | 0.5 NIGHT
    +5    | error   | 5 NIGHT   | 5 NIGHT

`u64::from_str` accepts a leading `+`, which is how the second row
happened without anyone writing it down. The same characters, typed into
two wallets from this project, meant two different amounts of money in
one case and an amount versus an error in the other. That is the
divergence the payment-request format exists to prevent on the wire,
arriving instead at the keyboard.

nightfall_wallet::amount_input is now the only one, and all three call
it. Its refusals name the mistake rather than gesturing at it: the
browser used to answer 99999999999999999999 with "not a number", which
teaches an owner that the wallet is broken rather than that the amount
is impossible, and 0 with "amount too small or too large". Amounts above
the whole supply are refused by name; the supply itself still parses.

Parsing stays on the characters and never goes through f64 — eight
decimal places do not survive binary floating point, and losing a dark
in a payment form is not a rounding error.

Also here: the payment-request format and its round-trip property, which
is what the wallets' "write a request" buttons rest on. A request is
built, read back with the parser a payer will use, and refused if it
does not come back identical, so the memo bound, the amount bound and
the encoding rules live in one place instead of on every screen.

head_commit.message:
One wrong word is not a missing word

Recovery had a single error variant reading "Enter this wallet's complete
24 recovery words". For a 23-word phrase that is good advice. For 24
words with one typo it is misleading in the worst direction: the owner
counts to 24, reads that the words are incomplete, and concludes the
wallet is broken rather than that they misread their own handwriting.

Worse, three code paths said three different things about that one
mistake — the web wallet said "Invalid recovery phrase.", the words check
on the create screen said the words were incomplete, and Core restore
said the checksum was wrong. None of them told the owner which of their
24 words to look at.

RecoveryError now splits into WrongLength(n) and NotAValidPhrase, and
recovery::keys_from_phrase is the single road in for the web wallet,

head_commit.message:
Encrypted wallet storage on Windows, and a CI job that proves it

The vault adapter refused to open at all unless `cfg!(unix)`, so Windows had
no encrypted wallet storage. It also had no test coverage of the adapter:
the workspace test run is Linux-only and the storage suite was gated to Unix,
while the Windows CI job only ever ran `cargo build`. A build says the code
compiles. It says nothing about whether the storage rules hold.

The per-platform calls now live in one place, `vault_fs`. Everything that
decides *when* a write is safe — the order, the checkpoints, the `unusable`
transitions, the verification after every write — stays shared, so a platform
cannot quietly acquire its own idea of it.

What Windows gets: CREATE_NEW for exclusive creation, FlushFileBuffers through
`sync_all`, an atomic replace via MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH, the
hard-link count read from the open handle rather than the path, and rejection
of every reparse point rather than only the links std reports as symlinks — a
cloud-storage placeholder is not a plain file either.

What it does not get, named rather than papered over:

  * No directory fsync. A directory cannot be opened for writing, so the
    rename asks to be written through instead — and Microsoft documents that
    flag for a copy-and-delete move, not for a rename inside one volume. The
    commit is atomic there; its durability is weaker than on Unix.
  * No file mode. Files inherit the profile directory's ACL, which keeps other
    users out on a normal install and does not keep out an administrator. This
    deliberately does not set a DACL of its own: an access-control path that
    cannot be tested reads like a guarantee, and would be worse than a gap
    that is written down.
  * No O_NOFOLLOW. The link check runs before the open; the moment between the
    two is a gap Unix closes and Windows leaves open.

ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION has no Unix counterpart and reads as gibberish on its
own, so it is translated: antivirus, backup and indexing tools hold files open,
and the message says so and says nothing was changed.

The storage suite is no longer gated to Unix. Thirty-five of its forty-four
cases now run on Windows, including all five crash-injection tests. The nine
that need symlinks or permission bits are marked `#[cfg(unix)]` in the source,
so the compiler drops them rather than a runner skipping them invisibly.

Verified before pushing: the Windows target compiles and is clippy-clean
against real Windows std and windows-sys; 72 wallet tests pass on macOS. Not
verified: an actual run on Windows. That is what the new CI step is for.

workflow_runs.display_title: 0.9.2 — the supply invariant stops walking the whole set

head_commit.message:
0.9.2 — the supply invariant stops walking the whole set

`commitment_sum` summed every commitment in the UTXO set by decompressing
each one, and `verify_supply_invariant` calls it once per block. That is
O(n) point decompressions per block and O(n²) over a chain, with n growing
— so it got worse every week. Measured on a running node: 1730 of 2302
stack samples inside verify_supply_invariant, 1599 of those in
CompressedRistretto::decompress.

Carried forward now: add on insert, subtract on remove. Every mutation
goes through those two methods, so it cannot drift behind the map's back.
The micro-benchmark in tests/sum_speed.rs reports the call as free.

The safety of that is the part worth reading. The obvious design — rebuild
the sum after loading — depends on every caller remembering to, and the
caller who forgets does not crash: it checks the supply invariant against
a sum over zero entries, which is the check silently switching itself off.
So a count of covered entries travels with the sum and is compared to the
map on every read; a deserialised set disagrees and gets the walking
version. Slow is recoverable, confidently wrong is not. Two tests pin it:
400 random insert/remove/re-insert/remove-absent steps against the
definition, and the deserialisation case explicitly.

Honest about the size of the win: this was one of three things that touch
the whole set per block. `self.ledger.clone()` copies the UTXO map and
`utxo_root()` rebuilds the Merkle tree, both still O(n) or worse per
block, and both now sit at the top of the profile. The floor underneath
all of it is real work — 95,867 memory-hard 32 MiB hashes is what "every
proof of work is re-derived" costs, and no optimisation removes it.

So the other half of this release is saying so while it happens. The
wallet shows a bar, a percentage and a remaining time measured from the
observed rate rather than a constant, and nightfalld logs progress every
five seconds instead of printing one line and going quiet for half an
hour. Every user who saw that silence reasonably concluded the process had
wedged.

Upgrading from 0.9.1 does not re-verify anything: the validation record's
trust fields are untouched. Demonstrated both ways — a datadir written by
this build reloads instantly, and the same datadir with validated_by
cleared logs "re-verifying proof of work for the whole chain".

head_commit.message:
0.9.1 — the wallet, redrawn against the phone

Seven tabs reworked to the style the phone wallet already had: flat cards,
one fill and one hairline border, values on the right edge of a list with
a rule between rows, headings tracked wide. The dashboard is untouched —
it was the reference.

Depth comes from the page, not the cards. Two very faint radial washes
across the top give the background somewhere to be lighter, so a flat card
has something to sit on. A first attempt gave every card a gradient and a
lit top edge; against the phone that reads as a seam, and eight of them
down a page read as a list of seams. Removed.

Send is three sections and a summary — recipient, amount, then the
numbers that decide the payment immediately above the button that commits
it. The total used to sit three fields higher, next to the amount, so the
last thing read before an irreversible action was a note about fee burning.

The fee chooser is gone. Economy, Standard and Priority differed in no way
the protocol can express: the fee is burned rather than paid to a miner,
and nothing in the node orders the mempool by it. "Priority" promised a
speed-up nothing delivers, which is worse than no choice at all — it makes
a slow payment look like the sender's mistake. One fee, as on the phone
and on the command line.

The rail's foot lost its floating box, and with it a lie: while the chain
loaded it showed a green dot beside the word "loading". Green there means
the supply sum was recomputed and balanced. Until it has been, the line is
dim.

Text fields got real padding. egui pads 4px horizontally, our inputs are
rounded to 12, so the first character sat on the corner arc — worst on the
short hints, "nf1…" and "optional". Nineteen fields, one constant.

Two checks were extended because this release walked into both gaps:
scripts/stamp-cache-busters.mjs required a leading slash and so silently
skipped index.html's src="js/main.js" — the file that fills in the download
buttons, which is exactly what shipped broken in 0.8.3. It now also fails
on any ?v= it does not manage. And check-web-wallet.mjs only asked that
sw.js had some number in its cache name, so a release could bump the
wallet's BUILD and leave every returning visitor on the old shell; the
cache name now has to carry the version.

Also in: the retired Vultr seed is out of seed-watch.sh and the Worker,
which had been fixed locally and never mirrored.

workflow_runs.display_title: Buttons inside a container were wearing the container's link colour

head_commit.message:
Buttons inside a container were wearing the container's link colour

"The text in the download button isn't really visible" turned out to be
specificity. `.btn-primary` is one class, (0,1,0). Any rule shaped
`.container a` is (0,1,1) and wins, so a button inside such a container
loses its white lettering and takes the container's link colour — on a
button filled with a bright gradient, that is text you cannot read.

Four rules had it, arrived at independently: .nav-links a, .doc a,
.foot-col a, .upfront-foot a. The chain page's archive button was violet
lettering on the violet gradient. Worse, .nav-links a repainted the site's
main Download button in --text-dim on every page, and had done so long
enough that nobody saw it any more: a button with unreadable text still
looks like a button, and the eye supplies the label it expects.

All four now say :not(.btn), which is the same guard the mobile nav rule
already used a few lines above. check-button-colours.mjs fails any future
`.container a` colour rule that does not, and is wired into CI — three
independent occurrences is a pattern, not an accident.

The stylesheet had the cache-buster problem too: style.css sat at a
hand-written ?v=live-7, and 404.html at ?v=live-5, so a CSS fix would have
reached nobody who had loaded the site before. The stamper now covers
stylesheets as well as scripts. Catching one and not the other would have
been the same mistake twice in one afternoon.

workflow_runs.display_title: The archive button stayed on one line and pushed the page off the phone

head_commit.message:
The archive button stayed on one line and pushed the page off the phone

`.btn` is white-space:nowrap, which is right for "Download" and wrong once
the archive's file name is appended to it. On a 375px screen the button
came out 513px wide, and the overflow gave the whole page a sideways
scrollbar rather than merely looking cramped.

The name now sits in its own element under the label, so the button
stacks into two lines and wraps. Measured at 375 and at 320, and with a
seven-digit height standing in for a chain far larger than this one: 288px
inside a 320px screen, no page overflow.

The cache busters are the real find behind it.

/js is served with max-age=86400, so ?v= is the only thing that tells a
returning browser to fetch again — and they were maintained by hand.
nav.js has sat at ?v=1 on five pages since it was written. chain.js was
pinned to the release version, which is stable by design and therefore
never changes when a page is fixed between releases. So this fix deployed,
was correct on the server, and ran in no browser that had loaded the page
earlier the same day. I only noticed because the button still rendered the
old label while the file on disk did not contain it.

scripts/stamp-cache-busters.mjs stamps each ?v= with the first eight hex
of the file's own sha256. It changes exactly when the file changes and
never when it does not, so an unchanged deploy keeps warm caches. --check
runs in CI. The version-based rule in check-chain-page.mjs is gone: it
fixed the failure it was written for and caused this one.

The browser wallet keeps its own scheme, where every buster must agree and
check-web-wallet.mjs enforces that.

workflow_runs.name: CI
workflow_runs.display_title: Never take the published archive down to put one up

head_commit.message:
Never take the published archive down to put one up

Running the whole thing end to end found what the pieces could not. The
chain had not moved while the wallet was closed, so the new archive had
the same <height>-<date> name as the published one, and `gh release upload
--clobber` deletes before it uploads. The download link on the live page
was a 404 for seven minutes — on a page whose own source says it must link
something real at every instant.

Two answers, because there are two cases.

Same name and the same bytes means the chain has not moved: nothing to
upload, nothing to deploy, say so and stop. Five seconds instead of eight
minutes, and the common case of running twice in a week no longer touches
anything.

Same name and different bytes — a reorg at the same height would do it —
uploads beside the live asset under a working name, then deletes the old
one and renames the new one into its place. The gap is one API call rather
than one upload.

That swap needs numeric asset ids from the REST API. `gh release view
--json assets` hands out GraphQL node ids, and the REST asset endpoints
answer those with a 404 that reads exactly like the asset is missing.
Tested against a throwaway draft release rather than the live one, which
is how the id mismatch turned up before it mattered.

The plain path no longer passes --clobber at all. If a name collides
without either branch catching it, better a loud failure than a silent
replacement.

workflow_runs.display_title: One command for the weekly chain archive

head_commit.message:
One command for the weekly chain archive

scripts/weekly-chain-archive.sh does the whole chore: build from the data
folder, replace last week's archive on the release, point the website at
it, deploy, then read the live site back the way a stranger would. Publish
and verify are not the same act, and only the second one is evidence.

It waits for the wallet instead of refusing. The copy needs nothing
writing to blocks.bin, so the script watches the OS lock, says what it is
waiting for, and announces the moment the wallet can go back up — the
upload, which is the slow part, does not need it. `--check` runs the
preflight alone, safe with the wallet open, so a stale login turns up
before anything is closed rather than after.

It replaces publish-chain-bootstrap.sh rather than joining it. Two scripts
doing the same upload is two scripts that drift; the systemd stop/start
survives as --service for an unattended archive node.

The retirement step is the part that needed a test. It sorted archive
names as strings, which is right until the height gains a digit: as text
"…-99981" sorts above "…-100248", so the newest archive would have sorted
last and been deleted by the run that had just uploaded it, leaving the
download page pointing at a file the script itself threw away. At 95,867
blocks that was roughly two weeks away. Now sorted on the height as a
number, with --self-test proving it on a fixture that contains exactly
that trap, wired into CI so it cannot come back.

The Cloudflare step checks the login wrangler actually uses. The previous
deploy passed CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN read from a file that does not exist on
this machine: the variable was empty, wrangler fell back to its own stored
login, and the deploy worked for a reason unlike the one written down.

head_commit.message:
Bootstrap instructions: Windows was missing, and so was the right hash tool

The section shipped with macOS and Linux only. Windows is the platform
whose users are least able to work out %APPDATA%\nightfall\mainnet\n8 on
their own, so it was missing exactly the audience that needed it.

The hash command was wrong for two of the three. `shasum` is a Perl
script: absent on Windows entirely, not guaranteed on a Linux box. Every
platform now gets the tool it actually has — Get-FileHash, shasum,
sha256sum — because a verification step that fails to run is a
verification step that gets skipped.

The checker now reads the artefacts in downloads/ and insists the page
covers every platform there. Ground truth is the files we ship, not a
list in the script that is one more thing to forget. Verified by removing
each platform in turn and watching it fail.

Also states what happens if the archive lands on a node that has already
synced: the byte count in the validation record no longer matches, the
fast path is refused, and the chain is re-checked from the start. Safe,
but pointless, and better said than discovered.

workflow_runs.name: CI
workflow_runs.display_title: Chain bootstrap: an archive newcomers can start from

head_commit.message:
Chain bootstrap: an archive newcomers can start from

Syncing from genesis is the first thing a new node does and the first
thing that makes someone close the wallet again. This publishes the chain
as one file, rebuilt weekly, and a section on /chain/ that describes it.

The archive ships blocks and nothing else. It deliberately omits
chain-meta.json, which is the file that records "this chain has been
validated". Shipping that would let a downloader skip the proof-of-work
check on 95k blocks they got from a URL — the archive would become a
statement to be trusted rather than data to be verified. Without it every
downloaded block is re-checked, exactly as if it had arrived from a peer.
The archive saves the network round-trips, not the verification.

That hole was real rather than theoretical, so the record is now bound to
the installation that produced it: chain-meta.json carries the install id
that validated it, and a record copied from elsewhere no longer counts as
our own. Four tests pin that down.

The publisher uploads the archive before the files that describe it, and
confirms it arrived. The first run did all three at once, the 158 MB
archive did not make it, and the release was left holding a checksum for
a file that did not exist — a download page reading that manifest would
have offered a dead link. It also keeps its work directory when a run
fails: rebuilding means taking a node down and copying the whole chain,
which is too expensive to throw away over a timed-out upload.

The datadir lock is checked through python3's fcntl rather than the flock
command, which is util-linux and absent on macOS; the first version of the
guard was silently skipped there and archived a live datadir.

workflow_runs.display_title: A consensus test that failed one run in sixty

head_commit.message:
A consensus test that failed one run in sixty

`assume_valid_never_reaches_a_chain_shorter_than_the_pin` broke a block's
proof of work by adding one to the nonce, then asserted the rebuild
refuses it. But a new nonce still meets the target with probability
1/difficulty, and the difficulty at that height is 60 — so about one run
in sixty handed the checker a block whose work was still perfectly valid
and then complained that it was accepted.

It bit the Windows runner on the v0.9.0 tag, which made it look like a
platform problem. It was a coin flip. Measured, not guessed: the
difficulty is printed by the same setup the test uses.

Now the test tampers until the work genuinely fails, and says so if no
such nonce exists — which is the case at difficulty 1, where this test
cannot mean anything and should say that rather than pass.
